q: Your support agent's loop sends Claude's request, runs any tool calls, and loops. A bug report shows it ran `process_refund` twice for one request. Logs show Claude's second response contained the same tool_use id the code had already handled. What's the most likely cause?
o: The code didn't append the tool_result for the first call, so Claude asked for the same tool again.
Claude randomly repeats tool calls, so the code should deduplicate every call by tool name alone.
`stop_reason` was "end_turn", which always means Claude wants the last tool to run once more.
The system prompt is too long, which makes Claude forget which tools it has already called.
e: When a tool runs but its tool_result never reaches the conversation history, Claude has no evidence the call happened and asks for it again. The fix is to append both the assistant's tool_use message and a matching tool_result before the next request. Deduplicating by tool name would block legitimate repeat calls, and "end_turn" means Claude is finished, not that it wants a rerun.

q: Your agent loop checks `stop_reason` after every response. Which value tells your code to execute the requested tools and send another request?
o: "tool_use"
"end_turn"
"max_tokens"
"stop_sequence"
e: "tool_use" means Claude is waiting for tool results, so the loop runs the tools, appends the results and continues. "end_turn" means Claude has finished. "max_tokens" means the reply was cut off by the token limit, and "stop_sequence" means a custom stop string was hit; neither asks for tools.

q: A response comes back with `stop_reason` "max_tokens" in the middle of a long research summary. How should your agent loop treat it?
o: As an incomplete response: raise the limit or ask Claude to continue, rather than treating it as done.
As a successful finish, because Claude always stops at a natural point before reaching the limit.
As a request for tools, so the loop should look for tool_use blocks and run them right away.
As a fatal error that should end the session and discard the partial summary that was written.
e: "max_tokens" means generation hit the output limit, so the text may stop mid-sentence. The loop should treat it as unfinished: continue the response or retry with a higher limit. It isn't a completion signal (that's "end_turn") or a tool request (that's "tool_use"), and throwing away useful partial work is wasteful.

q: Your coordinator decomposes "impact of AI on healthcare" into subtasks, but the final reports keep missing whole areas like regulation and insurance. Each subagent does its own part well. Where is the root cause most likely to be?
o: The coordinator's decomposition, which defined too narrow a set of subtasks for the topic.
The search subagent's tool descriptions, which make it pick the wrong search engine.
The synthesis subagent's prompt, which should invent missing sections when it sees gaps.
The model's context window, which is too small to hold findings from every subagent.
e: If every subagent does its assigned part well but whole areas are missing, the gap was created upstream when the coordinator chose the subtasks. Fix the decomposition (for example, have the coordinator enumerate the major dimensions of the topic first). Synthesis inventing sections would produce unsupported content, and nothing points to tool selection or context size.

q: Why do hub-and-spoke designs route all communication between subagents through the coordinator?
o: It gives one place to control information flow, handle errors, and observe what each agent did.
Subagents are technically unable to produce output unless a coordinator reformats it for them.
It lets every subagent see the full conversation history of every other agent automatically.
It removes the need for the coordinator to evaluate results, since subagents check each other.
e: Routing everything through the coordinator centralizes control: it decides what context each subagent gets, catches and handles failures, and gives you one place to observe and debug the flow. Subagents don't automatically share histories, and the coordinator still has to evaluate results rather than handing that off.

q: A user asks the research system a narrow question: "What year was the EU AI Act formally adopted?" How should a well-designed coordinator handle it?
o: Scale effort to the query: answer with a single quick search instead of spawning every subagent.
Always run the full pipeline of search, analysis, synthesis and report for consistent output.
Refuse the question, because multi-agent systems are only suited to open-ended research.
Spawn ten parallel search subagents so that the answer is confirmed by many separate sources.
e: A good coordinator adapts the plan to the query. A narrow factual question needs one quick lookup, not the full multi-agent pipeline, which adds cost and latency with no benefit. Refusing is unhelpful, and ten parallel searches is massive overkill for a single fact.

q: After synthesis, your coordinator reviews the draft and notices a key claim is backed by only one weak source. What's the best next step within the orchestration design?
o: Send a targeted follow-up task to a search subagent to find stronger evidence, then re-synthesize.
Publish the report as is, because the coordinator should never second-guess subagent output.
Delete the claim silently so the report only contains statements that have many sources.
Restart the entire research run from scratch with a different topic decomposition plan.
e: Iterative refinement is a core coordinator job: evaluate the output, find the gap, and delegate a focused follow-up rather than redoing everything. Publishing a weakly supported claim hurts quality, deleting it silently loses possibly true information, and a full restart wastes the work that was already good.

q: Your support system has a coordinator plus billing, shipping and account subagents. A customer's message touches only shipping. What's the best routing behavior?
o: Delegate only to the shipping subagent and skip the others for this request.
Call all three subagents in order every time so no possible issue is ever missed.
Have the billing subagent read the message first, since billing problems are most common.
Skip delegation and have the coordinator answer using whichever tools it has on hand.
e: The coordinator should route based on what the request actually needs. Calling every subagent on every message adds cost, latency, and chances for irrelevant output. A fixed "billing first" order ignores the content, and bypassing the specialist defeats the point of the design.

q: In the Claude Agent SDK, what must the coordinator agent have before it can spawn subagents?
o: The Task tool in its allowedTools, so it can invoke the subagents you have defined.
A shared memory file that every subagent reads automatically when the session starts.
A separate API key for each subagent, so the subagents can be billed independently.
The Bash tool, which it uses to launch each subagent as its own operating system process.
e: Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, so the coordinator's allowedTools must include it. Without Task, the coordinator has no way to delegate, even if AgentDefinitions exist. There's no automatic shared memory file, no per-subagent key, and subagents aren't launched through Bash.

q: Your coordinator spawned a synthesis subagent with the prompt "Write the final report." The report is generic and cites nothing. What's the most likely problem?
o: Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's context, so the findings had to be passed in the prompt.
The synthesis subagent needs a larger model, since generic writing means it lacks capability.
The prompt was too long, so the subagent ignored most of it and fell back on general knowledge.
Synthesis subagents can't cite sources unless they also have a web search tool to verify them.
e: Subagents start with isolated context. They only know what the coordinator puts in their prompt. A bare "Write the final report" gives synthesis nothing to work with, so it falls back on generic text. Pass the actual findings, with their sources, in the task prompt.

q: You want three search subagents to run at the same time instead of one after another. How should the coordinator request them?
o: Emit three Task tool calls in a single response, so they run in parallel.
Emit one Task call per turn and wait between them to avoid rate limits.
Ask a single subagent to pretend to be three agents in one long reply.
Put all three queries in the system prompt and let the model choose one.
e: Multiple Task tool calls in the same coordinator response let the subagents run in parallel. Spawning one per turn serializes them and multiplies wall-clock time. One subagent role-playing three loses the benefit of separate, focused contexts.

q: When passing web search results to the synthesis subagent, which format best preserves what synthesis needs?
o: Structured entries that keep each claim alongside its source URL, title and date.
A single paragraph summary of all findings, written to save as many tokens as possible.
Only the URLs, so the synthesis subagent can open each source and read it on its own.
The raw HTML of every page, so no information is lost on the way between the agents.
e: Synthesis needs content and provenance together. Structured entries that keep each claim tied to its source metadata let the report cite correctly. A merged paragraph loses attribution, bare URLs force redundant fetching, and raw HTML wastes context on markup.

q: Your coordinator's prompts to subagents spell out exact steps but never say what the result is for or what a good answer looks like. Subagents follow the steps yet return unhelpful output. What change helps most?
o: State the goal and the quality criteria, and let the subagent decide how to get there.
Add even more detailed steps so the subagent has no room to make its own decisions.
Remove all instructions and let the subagent work out the task from its tool list.
Ask the subagent to return its full reasoning so the coordinator can redo the work.
e: Good delegation describes the goal and what success looks like, not just procedures. A subagent that understands the purpose can adapt when the steps don't fit the material. Piling on steps makes it more brittle, and no instructions at all leaves it guessing.

q: You define an AgentDefinition for a "dependency-auditor" subagent. What does the definition specify?
o: Its description, its system prompt, and the tools it's allowed to use.
Only the model name, because subagents share the coordinator's tools.
The full history of the coordinator, which it receives automatically.
A schedule that controls when the subagent should wake up and run.
e: An AgentDefinition describes a subagent type: a description (so the coordinator knows when to use it), a system prompt, and tool restrictions. Subagents don't automatically get the coordinator's tools or history, and definitions aren't schedules.

q: The coordinator sends the same 30-page document to four subagents, but each only needs one section. What's the better approach?
o: Pass each subagent only the section and context relevant to its task.
Keep sending the full document so no subagent can ever miss a detail.
Send just the title and let each subagent search for the document itself.
Combine the four tasks into one subagent so the document is sent only once.
e: Give each subagent what its task needs. Sending the whole document four times wastes tokens and dilutes attention, while sending only a title forces redundant work. Merging the tasks throws away the focus that separate subagents provide.

q: Company policy says refunds must never be issued before the agent confirms the order belongs to the caller. Which approach gives a guarantee rather than a strong suggestion?
o: A programmatic gate that blocks `process_refund` until ownership has been verified.
A bold, capitalized rule at the top of the system prompt that repeats the policy.
Few-shot examples showing the agent verifying ownership before every refund.
A note in the `process_refund` description asking the agent to check first.
e: When a rule must always hold, enforce it in code. Prompts, examples and tool descriptions all make compliance more likely, but none guarantee it. A gate that refuses the refund call until verification succeeds makes the violation impossible.

q: Your agent escalates to a human, and the human agent's first message is always "Can you tell me what's going on?" What's missing from the handoff?
o: A structured summary: customer ID, issue, what was tried, and the reason for escalation.
A longer apology to the customer, explaining that a human will now take over the case.
The raw tool call logs, sent as-is, so the human can reconstruct the conversation.
A satisfaction survey, so the human knows how the customer feels about the agent.
e: Human agents usually can't see the transcript, so the handoff must carry the essentials in a compact, structured form. Raw logs are too noisy to read quickly, and an apology or survey doesn't tell the human what to do next.

q: A customer asks for an exchange, a refund on a different order, and an address change. What's the best way for the agent to handle the request?
o: Split it into the three issues, work through each, and confirm all three are resolved.
Handle only the first issue and ask the customer to open new chats for the other two.
Escalate immediately, because more than one issue in a message is always too complex.
Combine everything into one tool call so the systems process all three changes at once.
e: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed: identify each issue, resolve them (in parallel where independent), then confirm with the customer. Forcing separate chats is poor service, escalation isn't needed for routine items, and the tools act on one operation each.

q: Your gate requires `get_customer` before `lookup_order`. When Claude calls `lookup_order` first, what should the gate return?
o: A clear error saying the customer must be verified first, so Claude can call `get_customer`.
An empty success result, so the conversation flows on without interrupting the customer.
Nothing, and end the session, so the agent learns not to try the wrong order next time.
Fake order data, so the agent can keep going while verification happens in the background.
e: A good gate blocks the call and explains why, which lets Claude recover by doing the prerequisite step. Silent success or fake data would mislead the agent into wrong actions, and ending the session is a poor experience that doesn't teach the model anything.

q: Different tools return currency as cents, as dollar strings, and as floats. Which Agent SDK hook is the right place to convert them into one format before Claude reads them?
o: A PostToolUse hook, which can transform tool results before the model sees them.
A PreToolUse hook, which can rewrite the tool's output after the tool has finished.
A system prompt rule asking Claude to convert every currency value in its head.
A SessionStart hook, which converts all past and future values at the start.
e: PostToolUse hooks run after a tool executes and can normalize its result before the model processes it, which makes formats consistent everywhere. PreToolUse runs before the call, so it can't change output. Asking the model to convert values is error-prone.

q: Your coding agent must never push directly to the `main` branch. What's the most reliable control?
o: A PreToolUse hook that inspects Bash commands and blocks pushes to `main`.
A CLAUDE.md line that says "never push to main" in capital letters.
A PostToolUse hook that reports the push after it has already happened.
A friendly reminder in each prompt asking the agent to use feature branches.
e: PreToolUse hooks intercept a tool call before it runs and can deny it, so they enforce the rule deterministically. Instructions only make compliance likely, and a PostToolUse hook fires too late to prevent the push.

q: An engineer asks your agent to "migrate our logging from library A to library B." The call sites follow a few predictable patterns. Which decomposition fits best?
o: A fixed sequence: find all call sites, map each pattern to the new API, update, then run tests.
Fully open-ended exploration, letting the agent decide each next step from scratch every time.
One giant prompt asking for every file to be rewritten in a single response, all at once.
Ask the engineer to list every file by hand before the agent is allowed to do anything.
e: When the work is predictable, a fixed pipeline (prompt chaining) is reliable and easy to check. Open-ended, adaptive decomposition is better for investigations with unknown shape. A single giant response is error-prone, and pushing discovery onto the engineer wastes their time.

q: A user asks the research system to "figure out why our product's churn rose last quarter," with no clear starting point. Which decomposition approach fits best?
o: Adaptive: start with broad discovery, then create new subtasks based on what is found.
Fixed: run the same three searches every time, regardless of what they actually turn up.
None: answer from general knowledge about churn, without looking at any data at all.
Sequential: read every document in the company archive before forming any hypotheses.
e: Open-ended investigations benefit from dynamic decomposition, where each finding shapes the next subtasks. A fixed list can't follow leads, general knowledge ignores the actual data, and reading everything first is slow and unfocused.

q: Your CI review of a 40-file pull request gives shallow, inconsistent feedback in a single pass. Which decomposition improves depth and consistency?
o: Review each file in its own pass, then run a separate pass on how the files interact.
Review only the five largest files, since smaller files rarely contain real bugs.
Ask the reviewer to read the PR twice in the same pass and combine its thoughts.
Split the PR into 40 separate pull requests before allowing any review to run.
e: Splitting into per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass keeps each pass focused while still catching issues that span files. Skipping files misses bugs, re-reading in one pass doesn't fix attention dilution, and forcing 40 PRs is impractical.

q: Your extraction pipeline handles invoices, contracts and receipts. Each type needs different fields and checks. What's a sensible decomposition?
o: Classify the document type first, then route it to a type-specific extraction step.
Use one universal prompt with every field from every type marked as required.
Extract every document three times, once per type, and keep whichever output is longest.
Ask a human to sort the documents by type before the pipeline ever sees them.
e: A classify-then-route chain lets each step specialize. A universal prompt with every field required pressures the model to invent values, triple extraction wastes cost and picks results arbitrarily, and manual sorting removes the point of automation.

q: You want to try a risky refactor without losing your current Claude Code session's investigation. What lets you branch from where you are?
o: Fork the session, so the experiment gets its own copy of the history.
Run /clear, then paste the most important findings back in by hand.
Start a brand-new session and repeat the whole investigation again.
Keep going in the same session and undo everything later if needed.
e: Forking creates a new session that starts from the current history, so you can explore one approach while the original stays intact. /clear throws away context, a fresh session redoes work, and experimenting in place risks polluting the original line of work.

q: You named yesterday's Claude Code session "payments-audit". What does resuming it give you?
o: The earlier conversation history, so you can continue where you left off.
A fresh session that automatically re-reads every file in the repository.
Only the final message of yesterday's session, with the rest discarded.
A copy of yesterday's files exactly as they were on disk at the time.
e: Resuming a session restores its conversation history so you can continue the work. It doesn't snapshot files on disk or re-read the repo, so if files have changed since, you should tell Claude what changed.

q: You resume a session from two days ago. Since then, a teammate renamed a module that the session analyzed. What's the best practice?
o: Tell Claude specifically which files changed so it re-checks them before relying on old results.
Assume the old analysis still holds, because a resumed session updates itself automatically.
Delete the session and start over, because any change makes the whole history worthless.
Ask Claude to re-read the entire repository from scratch before continuing with any work.
e: A resumed session's tool results reflect the codebase at the time they were captured. Pointing Claude at the specific changes lets it re-analyze just those parts. Trusting stale results invites mistakes, while starting over or re-reading everything wastes the valid context.

q: Your old session's history is dominated by outdated tool outputs after a major rewrite. What's usually more reliable than resuming it?
o: Start a new session and give it a short summary of the key decisions and findings.
Resume it anyway and hope Claude notices which tool outputs are now out of date.
Fork it, because forking automatically refreshes every stale tool output inside.
Resume it with a larger context window so the stale results take up less space.
e: When most prior tool results are stale, a fresh session seeded with a concise summary avoids anchoring on outdated information. Forking copies the same stale history, and a bigger window doesn't make old results accurate.

q: Why might you fork a session twice from the same point?
o: To compare two different approaches that both start from the same shared analysis.
To double the context window available to the original session for later work.
To make Claude answer twice as fast by splitting the work across two sessions.
To create a backup in case the conversation history is deleted by accident.
e: Forking twice from one point gives you two independent branches with the same starting context, which is ideal for comparing alternatives side by side. Forks don't add context capacity to the original or speed up generation.

q: A long-running exploration session in Claude Code is getting slow and starts repeating itself. You still need its main conclusions for the next task. What's a good approach?
o: Summarize the key findings, then continue in a fresh session that starts from that summary.
Keep working in the same session, since slowdowns go away once the context gets larger.
Fork the session repeatedly, so each fork carries a little less of the history forward.
Close the session and rely on memory, since conclusions are easy to rediscover later.
e: Carrying a concise summary into a new session keeps the conclusions while dropping the noise that's degrading performance. A growing context makes things worse, forks copy the full history, and rediscovering findings wastes effort.

q: Your support agent has `get_order` ("Gets order") and `get_shipment` ("Gets shipment"). It often calls `get_order` when customers ask where their package is. What's the most effective first fix?
o: Expand both descriptions: what each returns, example questions, and when to use the other one.
Merge both tools into one `get_order_or_shipment` tool, since two similar tools will always confuse the model.
Add a few-shot example to the system prompt showing one correct shipment lookup.
Rename `get_shipment` to `zz_get_shipment` so the model notices it is different.
e: Tool descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose a tool. Minimal descriptions give it nothing to tell the tools apart. Spelling out inputs, outputs, example queries and boundaries is the cheapest, most direct fix. Merging may be unnecessary, and odd names add no meaning.

q: Which detail is most useful to include in a web search tool's description?
o: What kinds of queries it handles well, what it returns, and its known limits.
The name of the engineer who built it and the date it was last deployed.
A reminder that the tool is very important and should be used frequently.
The internal URL of the search service and the port number it listens on.
e: A tool description should help Claude decide when and how to use the tool: the purpose, input expectations, output shape, and limitations. Authorship, emphatic urging, and infrastructure details don't help with tool selection.

q: Your agent has `read_config` and `read_file`, and it uses `read_file` on config files, which skips validation. What's the best way to steer it?
o: Say in `read_config`'s description that it's for config files, and in `read_file`'s to use `read_config` for those.
Remove `read_file` from the agent entirely, so that config files can only ever be opened through `read_config` and nothing else.
Add a hook that silently rewrites every `read_file` call into a `read_config` call, without the model ever knowing about it.
Lower the temperature so the model makes the same tool choice more consistently.
e: Clear boundaries in both descriptions (including when to use the other tool) are the direct fix for overlapping tools. Removing `read_file` breaks legitimate uses, silently rewriting calls hides the problem, and temperature doesn't fix ambiguity in the descriptions.

q: Your extraction tool takes a `document_type` parameter, but the model often passes values like "bill" or "statement" that your code doesn't accept. What helps most?
o: Define the parameter as an enum of accepted values and describe what each one means.
Leave the parameter as free text and reject any call that uses an unexpected value.
Remove the parameter and have your code guess the document type from the file name.
Ask the model in the system prompt to try harder to pick the right value each time.
e: An enum in the input schema, with each value explained, tells the model exactly which values are valid and when to use them. Rejecting free text after the fact causes retries, guessing from file names is unreliable, and "try harder" adds no information.

q: Two tools, `summarize_text` and `extract_claims`, are both described as "Processes a document." What's the core problem?
o: The descriptions don't say how the tools differ, so Claude can't choose between them.
The tools have different names, which confuses the model about what each does.
The model can only use one document tool per conversation, so one will be ignored.
The descriptions are too short to be shown to the model and are dropped entirely.
e: Identical, vague descriptions remove the information Claude needs to pick the right tool. Each description should explain what the tool does differently and when to use it.

q: You add a new `check_warranty` tool, but the agent keeps answering warranty questions from its general knowledge instead. What's the most likely fix?
o: Describe in the tool when it should be used, e.g. any question about warranty status or coverage.
Delete the agent's general knowledge so it has no choice but to use the new tool.
Move `check_warranty` to the top of the tools list, because the order of tools decides which one Claude tries first.
Force `tool_choice` to `check_warranty` for every request the agent receives.
e: If the description doesn't make the tool's purpose and trigger situations clear, Claude may not realize it should use it. Order in the list isn't a reliable priority mechanism, and forcing the tool on every request would break all other conversations.

q: Which description is best for a `search_logs` tool?
o: "Searches application logs by time range and keyword. Returns up to 100 matching lines with timestamps. Use for debugging runtime errors, not for source code."
"Searches logs."
"A powerful, essential, cutting-edge log searching tool that every agent needs. It is extremely important, so use it as often as you possibly can."
"Calls the internal log search service (v2.3), which is maintained by the infrastructure team and was last updated in March of this year."
e: A good description states inputs, outputs, limits and when (and when not) to use the tool. The short one gives no guidance, the hyped one adds no facts, and the last one describes ownership rather than behavior.

q: Your MCP server exposes a tool named `do_task` with the description "Does the task." Developers report Claude rarely uses it. Why?
o: The name and description give Claude no way to know what the tool does or when it fits.
MCP tools are only used when the user types the tool's exact name into the prompt.
Claude avoids any tool whose name contains a verb, preferring tools named as nouns.
Claude limits itself to built-in tools and ignores MCP tools unless forced to use them.
e: Claude chooses tools based on their names and descriptions. A vague name plus an empty description makes the tool impossible to match to a request. Rename it and describe its purpose, inputs and outputs.

q: Your schema for `extract_receipt` has a field named `amt`. The model sometimes fills it with the tax amount instead of the total. What's the best fix?
o: Give the field a clear name and description, such as `total_amount`: final amount paid including tax.
Remove the field from the schema and calculate the receipt total in your own code from the scanned receipt image.
Add `amt` to the required list, so the model takes the field more seriously.
Ask the model to double-check all fields in a second request after each extraction.
e: Field names and descriptions are part of the instructions the model reads. An ambiguous abbreviation invites wrong mappings. Clear naming and a short description resolve it. Marking the field required doesn't clarify its meaning.

q: Your research agent has `search_news` and `search_papers`. For a question about recent clinical trial results, which description change would best guide it to use both?
o: State in each description what kind of sources it covers, so Claude sees both are relevant.
Merge the two into one tool named `search_everything`, with a one-line description.
Add "ALWAYS USE THIS TOOL" to the start of both descriptions to make them stand out.
Remove `search_news`, since academic papers are always more reliable than the news.
e: When descriptions clearly state the coverage of each tool, Claude can see a question needs both. Merging hides the distinction, "ALWAYS" statements create conflicts, and dropping a useful source narrows coverage.

q: How should an MCP tool tell the agent that a call failed, rather than returning normal data?
o: Return a result with `isError` set to true and a clear message about what went wrong.
Return an empty string, so the agent assumes nothing was found and moves on.
Crash the MCP server, so the client knows that something serious has happened.
Return normal-looking data with a hidden flag the model is told to look for.
e: MCP tool results have an `isError` flag for this purpose. Setting it, with a useful message, lets the agent recognize the failure and respond appropriately. Empty strings look like valid "no results", crashing is disruptive, and hidden flags are unreliable.

q: `update_address` fails because the new postal code is invalid. Which error response helps the agent most?
o: A validation error explaining that the postal code is invalid and what format is expected.
A generic "Something went wrong, please try again later" message for every failure.
A retryable timeout error, so that the agent tries the same request a few more times.
A success response, while your code quietly logs the problem for an engineer to review.
e: A specific validation error tells the agent the input was wrong and how to fix it, so it can ask the customer for the correct code. A generic message prompts pointless retries, mislabeling it as a timeout invites the same failure again, and fake success misleads the customer.

q: Which error categories help an agent decide what to do after a tool fails?
o: Transient, validation, business-rule, and permission errors, each with whether retrying makes sense.
Red, yellow and green severities, with red meaning the agent should stop all work at once.
Errors from the tool and errors from the model, since that's the only distinction that matters.
Numeric codes only, since the model can look up the meaning of each code by itself later.
e: Different failure types call for different responses: retry transient errors, fix input for validation errors, explain business-rule rejections, and escalate or ask for access on permission errors. Including whether a retry makes sense helps the agent avoid pointless loops.

q: `process_refund` rejects a request because refunds over $1,000 need manager approval. What should the error tell the agent?
o: That a business rule blocked it, that retrying won't help, and that escalation is the next step.
That the service is temporarily unavailable, so the agent should retry in a few minutes.
Only the word "denied", so customers don't learn about the internal approval threshold.
That the refund succeeded, while your code quietly sends the request to a manager queue.
e: A business-rule failure is not retryable. Saying so, and pointing to escalation, lets the agent explain the situation and hand off correctly. Calling it transient causes useless retries, a bare "denied" gives no path forward, and fake success is dishonest.

q: A search subagent's query hits a rate limit. What's the best handling?
o: Retry locally with a short backoff, and report to the coordinator only if it still fails.
Immediately report total failure so the coordinator cancels the whole research task.
Return an empty result set, which the coordinator will treat as "nothing was found".
Switch to answering from general knowledge without telling the coordinator anything.
e: Transient errors like rate limits should be retried where they happen. Only if recovery fails should the subagent report a structured error with what was tried. Returning empty results or silently switching sources hides the failure and corrupts the research.

q: `lookup_order` returns no order for the number the customer gave. How should the tool respond?
o: A normal, successful result saying no order matches, distinct from an error.
An `isError` result with a message saying the order database has crashed.
A transient error, so the agent retries the same order number several times.
A random recent order, so the agent always has something to show the customer.
e: "Not found" is a valid answer, not a failure. Returning it as a successful empty result lets the agent ask the customer to double-check the number. Labeling it an outage or a transient error leads to wrong messages and pointless retries.

q: Your agent keeps retrying a tool that fails with "permission denied" for the current user. What should the tool's error include to stop this?
o: A permission error category marked as not retryable, with a note on how access can be granted.
A higher retry limit, so the agent has more attempts before it finally gives up for good.
A message that says "try again", so the agent knows that the failure isn't its own fault.
Nothing extra, since the model can always work out on its own whether retries will help.
e: Marking the error as non-retryable, with its category and a hint for resolution, tells the agent to stop retrying and take the right next step. Encouraging retries or raising the limit just wastes calls on a failure that will not change.

q: A subagent's document fetch fails after it has already analyzed 8 of 10 documents. What should it return to the coordinator?
o: The 8 completed analyses plus a structured note on the 2 failures and what was attempted.
Nothing, since partial results are confusing and the coordinator prefers all-or-nothing.
Only the error, so the coordinator restarts the whole subagent task from the beginning.
All 10 analyses, with the missing 2 filled in from what the titles appeared to suggest.
e: Return the partial results together with clear information about what failed. That lets the coordinator decide whether to retry the failures or proceed. Throwing away good work is wasteful, and inventing missing analyses corrupts the output.

q: Your `charge_card` tool returns "Error 402" on a declined card. The agent tells the customer the system is broken. What's the fix?
o: Return a descriptive error explaining the card was declined and that the customer can try another card.
Teach the model every HTTP status code in the system prompt so it can decode each one correctly on its own.
Hide card declines from the agent and always report a generic error to the customer instead.
Retry the charge automatically up to ten times before telling the agent anything at all.
e: Bare error codes leave the model to guess. A descriptive message that explains the failure and the next step lets the agent respond accurately. Retrying a declined card repeatedly could cause real harm.

q: You always want the model to call `extract_invoice`, never to reply with text. Which `tool_choice` setting guarantees that?
o: `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`
`"auto"`
`"none"`
No `tool_choice` at all, relying on the default
e: Forcing a specific tool by name guarantees Claude calls that tool. "auto" lets the model decide whether to use tools or reply in text, "none" prevents tool use, and the default behaves like "auto".

q: Your extraction step has three tools (invoices, receipts, contracts). You need the model to call one of them but not reply with text. Which setting fits?
o: `tool_choice: "any"`, which requires some tool call but lets the model choose which.
`tool_choice: "auto"`, which always guarantees at least one of the tools is called.
Forcing `extract_invoice` by name, then rejecting results that aren't invoices.
Removing all tools, and asking the model to reply in JSON text instead of tools.
e: "any" requires the model to call a tool while still letting it pick the right one. "auto" allows a text-only reply, forcing one tool by name removes the choice, and dropping tools loses schema enforcement.

q: Your web search subagent also has file write, email and database tools it never needs. What's the main benefit of removing them?
o: Fewer, role-specific tools make tool selection more reliable and reduce the risk of misuse.
Removing tools makes the subagent's model larger and more capable at searching the web.
Tools that are never used cost nothing, so removing them has no real benefit at all.
The subagent will then be able to call tools that belong to other subagents instead.
e: Giving each agent only the tools its role needs narrows the choice, which improves selection, and limits what can go wrong. Extra tools add confusion and risk even if they're rarely called.

q: Your team wants everyone who clones the repo to get the same MCP servers in Claude Code. Where should they be configured?
o: In `.mcp.json` at the project root, committed to the repository.
In each developer's `~/.claude.json`, set up individually by hand.
In the README, as instructions that each developer follows manually.
In a CLAUDE.md file, written as a list of servers to connect to.
e: Project-scoped MCP servers live in `.mcp.json`, which is checked in so every clone gets them. `~/.claude.json` is user-level (personal), a README depends on manual setup, and CLAUDE.md is for instructions, not server configuration.

q: Your `.mcp.json` needs an API token for a shared server. How should the token be handled?
o: Reference an environment variable like `${API_TOKEN}` so the secret isn't committed.
Paste the token directly into `.mcp.json`, since the repository is private anyway.
Put the token in CLAUDE.md, where Claude can read it when it needs to connect.
Email the token to each developer and ask them to edit the file before each use.
e: `.mcp.json` supports environment variable expansion, so the file can be shared while each developer supplies the secret locally. Committing secrets, even to private repos, is risky, and CLAUDE.md is loaded into context, which is no place for credentials.

q: What's the difference between MCP tools and MCP resources?
o: Tools perform actions the model calls; resources expose data the client can read as context.
Tools only work in Claude Code, while resources only work when you call the Messages API directly.
Resources are just tools that have been marked as deprecated by the server author.
There's no real difference; the two words are interchangeable names for one thing.
e: MCP tools are callable operations. Resources expose content (documents, schemas, catalogs) that can be loaded as context, which can save the agent exploratory tool calls. Both are part of the protocol and usable across clients.

q: Your team needs Claude Code to work with a popular, well-known service. A community MCP server for it already exists and is maintained. What's the recommended approach?
o: Use the existing server, and build a custom one only for team-specific workflows.
Always write your own server from scratch so you fully understand all of its code.
Avoid MCP and paste data from the service into the chat whenever it's needed.
Ask Claude to scrape the service's website each time instead of using a server.
e: For standard integrations, an existing, maintained MCP server saves time. Custom servers make sense for workflows unique to your team. Copy-pasting or scraping is fragile and manual.

q: A developer adds an MCP server with user scope. Who can use it?
o: Only that developer, across their projects, because it's stored in their user config.
Everyone on the team, because user-scope servers are synced to teammates through the repository.
No one, until the server is also listed in the project's CLAUDE.md file.
Only CI pipelines, since user scope is reserved for automated environments.
e: User-scoped MCP servers live in the developer's own configuration (`~/.claude.json`) and are available to them across projects, but aren't shared with teammates. Sharing happens through the project's `.mcp.json`.

q: You need to find every file that contains the string `LEGACY_API_KEY`. Which built-in tool is the best fit?
o: Grep, which searches file contents for a pattern.
Glob, which matches file paths against patterns.
Read, opening each file one at a time to check.
Write, creating a file that lists the matches.
e: Grep searches inside files for text or patterns, which is exactly this task. Glob finds files by name or path, Read is for viewing a specific file, and Write creates files.

q: You need all files under `src/` whose names end in `.config.ts`. Which built-in tool fits best?
o: Glob with a pattern like `src/**/*.config.ts`.
Grep searching for the text `.config.ts` in every file.
Read on the `src/` folder to print all of its contents.
Edit to rename all files so they're easier to find.
e: Glob matches file paths by pattern. Grep searches file contents, so it would find mentions of the string rather than the files themselves. Read opens files, and Edit changes content.

q: Claude's Edit fails twice because the target text isn't unique in a large file. What's a reasonable fallback?
o: Read the file, then write the full corrected version with Write.
Keep retrying the same Edit until the tool happens to succeed.
Delete the file and ask the developer to rewrite it by hand.
Use Grep to change the text, since Grep can modify matches.
e: When Edit can't find a unique anchor, reading the file and writing the corrected content is a reliable fallback. Repeating a failing call won't help, Grep only searches, and deleting work is drastic.

q: To understand how a feature works in an unfamiliar repo, what's the most efficient exploration pattern?
o: Grep for entry points, then Read the files they lead to, following imports as needed.
Read every file in the repository first, from top to bottom in alphabetical order.
Use Glob to list all files, then guess the answer from the file and folder names.
Ask the model to write the feature from scratch and compare it to what's in the repo.
e: Targeted search followed by focused reading builds understanding incrementally without flooding context. Reading everything wastes context, file names alone are too thin, and rewriting the feature doesn't explain the existing code.

q: Your agent needs to run the project's test suite and see the results. Which built-in tool does that?
o: Bash, which runs shell commands such as the test command.
Read, which opens the test files and reports what they do.
Grep, which searches the tests for the word "pass".
Glob, which lists all test files that exist in the repo.
e: Running a program, such as a test command, requires Bash. Read, Grep and Glob only look at files; they can't execute anything or produce real test results.

q: Your team's testing conventions are in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the tech lead's machine. Teammates' sessions don't follow them. Why?
o: That file is user-level, so it only applies to the tech lead; team rules belong in the project's CLAUDE.md.
Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md files only on the first day a repository is cloned onto a machine.
User-level files override project files, so each teammate's own personal settings are hiding the team's conventions.
Conventions only work when they're written as hooks, and CLAUDE.md is ignored for testing rules.
e: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is personal configuration on one machine. Shared conventions should go in the project-level CLAUDE.md (or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) committed to the repo, so everyone's sessions load them.

q: Your project CLAUDE.md is getting long. How can you split it into topic files and still have them loaded?
o: Move topics into separate files and reference them from CLAUDE.md with `@` imports.
Split the file into several CLAUDE.md files and put them all in the project root.
Move everything to the README, which Claude Code reads in place of CLAUDE.md.
Paste the topic files into the chat at the start of every session by hand.
e: CLAUDE.md supports `@path/to/file` imports, so you can keep focused topic files and pull them in from the main file. Multiple files with the same name can't share a folder, the README isn't a memory file, and pasting by hand is error-prone.

q: The `packages/billing/` folder needs extra instructions that only matter when working in that package. Where's a good place for them?
o: A CLAUDE.md file inside `packages/billing/`, which applies when working there.
The user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file of every developer on the team.
The top of the root CLAUDE.md, marked as "billing only" in capital letters.
A comment at the top of each billing source file that Claude might open.
e: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files scope instructions to that part of the codebase. User-level files aren't shared, a root file loads everywhere, and scattered code comments aren't a reliable way to configure Claude.

q: Where should a custom slash command live so that every developer on the project gets it?
o: In `.claude/commands/` inside the repository, committed to version control.
In `~/.claude/commands/` on whichever developer's machine created the command.
In CLAUDE.md, written as a paragraph that describes what the command should do.
In the project's `package.json`, under a new section named `claudeCommands`.
e: Project commands in `.claude/commands/` are shared through the repo. `~/.claude/commands/` is personal, CLAUDE.md holds instructions rather than command definitions, and `package.json` isn't where Claude Code looks.

q: Your `/explore-schema` skill dumps long exploration output into the main session. Which SKILL.md frontmatter option keeps that output out of your main context?
o: `context: fork`, which runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context.
`allowed-tools: none`, which stops the skill from producing any output.
`argument-hint`, which tells the skill to keep its responses short.
`model: small`, which makes the skill's output use fewer tokens.
e: `context: fork` runs the skill in a separate context, so only its result returns to the main conversation. `allowed-tools` restricts tools, `argument-hint` prompts for arguments, and a model choice doesn't isolate output.

q: You want database migration conventions to load only when Claude edits files in `db/migrations/`. What's the best setup?
o: A file in `.claude/rules/` with `paths: ["db/migrations/**/*"]` in its frontmatter.
A section at the bottom of the root CLAUDE.md titled "Migration conventions".
A personal note in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on each developer's own machine.
A `/migrations` slash command each developer has to remember to run first.
e: Rules in `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` glob load only when Claude works on matching files, keeping the conventions relevant and out of context otherwise. Root CLAUDE.md loads everywhere, personal files aren't shared, and a command relies on people remembering.

q: You need to fix a typo in an error message in one file. Which approach fits?
o: Direct execution: make the edit right away.
Plan mode: explore the codebase and draft a plan first.
Spawn subagents to review the change in parallel.
Write an architecture document before editing.
e: Small, clear, single-file changes are a good fit for direct execution. Planning, parallel review, or design documents add overhead with no benefit for a typo.

q: You're asked to replace the app's authentication system, which touches dozens of files and has several possible designs. Which approach fits?
o: Start in plan mode to explore and agree on an approach, then implement.
Start editing immediately and adjust the design as problems appear.
Ask Claude for the whole change in one response without looking first.
Skip Claude for this task, because large changes can't use plan mode.
e: Large, multi-file changes with open design choices benefit from plan mode: explore safely, compare approaches, and agree on one before editing. Diving in risks costly rework.

q: In plan mode, what does Claude do?
o: Explore and analyze the codebase and propose a plan, without making changes yet.
Make every change at once, then show a plan of what it has already finished.
Only run tests, so you can see which parts of the codebase are failing now.
Write a plan into CLAUDE.md, which it then follows in every future session.
e: Plan mode is for read-only exploration and planning. Claude investigates and proposes an approach, and changes happen only after you approve moving to execution.

q: You're planning a refactor and the discovery step would flood your session with search output. What helps keep your main context clean?
o: Delegate the discovery to a subagent (such as Explore) and keep only its summary.
Turn off all tools so the discovery step can't produce any output at all.
Run discovery in the main session, then use /clear to delete everything after.
Skip discovery and start the refactor based on what you remember of the code.
e: A subagent can do the verbose exploration in its own context and return a concise summary. Disabling tools blocks the work, clearing loses the findings, and skipping discovery risks a wrong plan.

q: You want Claude to write a function that parses messy addresses. What's the most effective way to define what "correct" means?
o: Write test cases first, including tricky inputs, and have Claude iterate until they pass.
Describe the goal in one sentence and accept the first version Claude writes.
Ask Claude to decide for itself what correct output looks like and to grade its own work.
Write the function yourself first and only ask Claude to add the code comments.
e: Tests make expectations concrete, cover edge cases, and give Claude a clear signal to iterate against. A single sentence leaves too much to interpretation, and self-grading without criteria is weak.

q: Your prose instructions for a date-normalizing function keep being misread. What's the most effective way to clarify?
o: Give a few concrete input and expected-output examples.
Repeat the same prose instructions, but in capital letters.
Make the prose instructions twice as long with more detail.
Ask Claude to guess and then correct the result yourself.
e: Concrete input/output examples remove ambiguity faster than more prose. Shouting or lengthening the same description rarely fixes misunderstanding.

q: You're unsure how best to add rate limiting to an API you don't know well. What should you do before Claude writes code?
o: Have Claude ask you clarifying questions about requirements and constraints first.
Tell Claude to pick any approach, since rate limiting is always the same everywhere.
Ask Claude to implement five different approaches and keep all of them in the code.
Avoid using Claude, since it can't help unless you already know the full solution.
e: When requirements are uncertain, an interview-style pass where Claude asks questions surfaces constraints you may not have thought of. Picking blindly or implementing five versions creates waste.

q: You found four independent bugs in different parts of a module. How should you give them to Claude?
o: Fix them one at a time with clear feedback for each, since they don't affect each other.
Hide three of them, because Claude can only ever work on a single bug per session.
Describe all four vaguely in one sentence, so Claude has room to find them itself.
Ask Claude to rewrite the whole module from scratch rather than fixing anything.
e: Independent issues can be handled sequentially with specific feedback, which keeps each fix focused. Interacting issues are better given together, but these don't interact. Vague descriptions and full rewrites add risk.

q: Claude's fix works for most inputs but breaks on empty lists. What's the most effective feedback?
o: Give the failing input, the actual output, and the expected output.
Say "it doesn't work, please try again" and wait for a new version.
Ask Claude to add more comments explaining the code to the reader.
Revert everything and start over with a brand-new prompt.
e: Specific failing cases with actual vs. expected results give Claude exactly what it needs to fix the edge case. Vague feedback leads to guesswork, and comments or restarts don't fix the bug.

q: Your CI step runs Claude Code but hangs waiting for input. Which flag runs it non-interactively?
o: `-p` (print mode)
`--verbose`
`--resume`
`--continue`
e: `-p` runs Claude Code in non-interactive print mode, which processes the prompt and exits, as a pipeline needs. `--verbose` changes logging, and `--resume`/`--continue` pick up previous sessions.

q: Your pipeline needs Claude Code's review output in a form scripts can parse. Which option helps most?
o: `--output-format json`, ideally with a JSON schema for the findings.
Plain text output, parsed afterwards with a set of regular expressions.
Asking Claude in the prompt to "please be machine readable".
Writing output to a log file and having a human copy the results.
e: JSON output (and a schema for the structure of findings) gives scripts something reliable to parse. Regex over prose breaks easily, and polite requests don't guarantee a format.

q: How can you give Claude Code in CI your team's review standards without putting them in every prompt?
o: Put them in the project's CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads automatically in CI too.
Pass them in through an environment variable named `CLAUDE_STANDARDS`.
Store them in the CI provider's secret store, where Claude Code looks first.
Skip them, since Claude Code learns your standards from previous pull requests.
e: Claude Code reads the project's CLAUDE.md in CI just as it does locally, so project conventions are picked up automatically. There's no special environment variable or secret store lookup for standards, and it doesn't learn from past PRs.

q: Your CI review runs on every push and keeps re-posting comments on issues already reported. What's a good fix?
o: Include the existing review comments in context and ask it to report only new or unresolved issues.
Delete all of the previous review comments before every run, so the new results replace them cleanly.
Run the review only once per week, so there are fewer runs that can post duplicates.
Turn off review comments and send the findings to a log file that nobody needs to read.
e: Giving the reviewer the prior findings lets it avoid repeating them and focus on new or still-open issues. Deleting history loses discussion, weekly runs miss problems, and hiding results defeats the purpose.

q: Why is a separate Claude Code session better for reviewing code than the session that wrote it?
o: A fresh session doesn't share the writer's reasoning, so it's less likely to overlook the same mistakes.
Each session can only use a given tool once, so the writer session has already used up its review tool.
The writer session is locked once it has made edits, so it can't open any files for a review at all.
Fresh sessions use a different, larger model by default, so they're better at reading the code.
e: A session that generated code carries its own assumptions and tends to confirm them. An independent session reviews with fresh eyes. There's no single-use tool limit, edit lock, or automatic model change.

q: Your CI test-generation step keeps writing tests for behavior that's already covered. What helps most?
o: Give it the existing tests in context, so it can focus on what's missing.
Ask for twice as many tests, so some of them are more likely to be new.
Delete the existing tests so there is nothing left for the new ones to duplicate.
Run test generation less often, so there are fewer duplicates overall.
e: If the generator can see current tests, it can target uncovered behavior. Asking for more tests or deleting existing ones doesn't address the cause.

q: Your review prompt says "flag anything that could be improved." Developers complain about noise. Which rewrite reduces false positives most?
o: List the specific issue types to report (e.g. bugs, security risks) and the ones to skip (e.g. style preferences).
Add "only flag important things" to the end of the existing prompt so the model knows to be selective.
Ask the model to give each finding a confidence score from 0 to 100 and keep only those it rates as above 50 percent.
Keep the prompt the same, but post the comments less often so developers notice the noise less.
e: Explicit categories of what to report and what to skip give the model concrete criteria. Vague qualifiers like "important" don't change behavior much, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.

q: A review category has so many false positives that developers ignore all findings. What's a reasonable short-term step?
o: Temporarily disable that category while you improve its criteria, to restore trust.
Keep it on and add more categories so the noisy one stands out less among them.
Make every finding from that category show up as critical so that people read it.
Ask developers to read every comment carefully, no matter how noisy it seems.
e: Noise in one category erodes trust in all of them. Turning it off while you fix its criteria protects the useful categories. Inflating severity or adding categories makes the noise problem worse.

q: Your extractor handles standard invoices well but fails on ones where the total appears only in a footnote. What's the most effective fix?
o: Add a few-shot example showing a footnote total and how to extract it correctly.
Tell the model to "look carefully everywhere" at the start of the prompt.
Remove the total field so the model no longer fails on that one document type.
Lower the temperature to zero so the model reads every invoice more carefully.
e: Few-shot examples of the tricky format show the model exactly how to handle it. Generic instructions to look harder don't teach the pattern, and dropping the field avoids the problem rather than solving it.

q: You want review comments in a consistent format: file, line, issue, why it matters, and a fix. What's most effective?
o: Include two or three example comments in that exact format.
Describe the format once in a long paragraph of prose.
Let the model choose a format and then reformat it in code.
Ask for the format in capital letters at the top of the prompt.
e: Examples are the most reliable way to get a consistent output format. Prose descriptions leave room for drift, and fixing format in code after the fact is fragile.

q: Your support agent handles clear refund requests well but is inconsistent on borderline ones. What kind of few-shot examples help most?
o: Borderline cases, each showing the decision and the reasoning behind it.
Many more clear-cut cases, to reinforce the behavior that already works.
Examples from unrelated domains, so the model learns general reasoning.
A single example, since more than one example confuses the model.
e: Examples that target the ambiguous cases, with the reasoning shown, teach the model how to make the judgment calls it gets wrong. More easy examples add little, and unrelated domains don't transfer the specific policy.

q: Why include examples of documents with missing fields in your extraction prompt?
o: They show the model to return null for missing data instead of making up a value.
They make the model skip any document that has a missing field entirely.
They reduce token usage, since documents with missing fields are shorter.
They let the model fill missing fields from earlier documents in the batch.
e: Showing examples where the right answer is null teaches the model that absence is acceptable, which reduces hallucinated values. Skipping documents or borrowing values from other documents would be wrong.

q: Your few-shot examples for code review all come from Python files, and reviews of TypeScript files are much weaker. What's the best fix?
o: Add varied examples that cover the languages and patterns the reviewer actually sees.
Convert every TypeScript file to Python before the reviewer is allowed to see it.
Remove all examples, since examples only ever help with one programming language.
Add more Python examples, since the model will generalize them to other languages.
e: Few-shot examples work best when they reflect the variety of real inputs. Examples from just one language leave the model unsure how to apply the judgment elsewhere.

q: What does defining an extraction tool with a JSON schema and having Claude call it give you?
o: Output that follows the schema's structure, which avoids JSON syntax errors.
A guarantee that every value extracted is factually correct for the document.
Automatic checks that totals add up and that dates fall in the right range.
A way to skip validation in your code, since the model can't make mistakes.
e: Tool use with a schema reliably produces well-formed output in the right shape. It doesn't guarantee the values are correct or consistent, so semantic checks (like totals adding up) still belong in your code.

q: Some contracts don't have a renewal date. Your schema marks `renewal_date` as required, and the model invents dates. What's the fix?
o: Make `renewal_date` nullable or optional, so the model can say it's absent.
Keep it required and add "never make up dates" in capital letters.
Remove the field and ask a human to add renewal dates later by hand.
Default it to today's date in code whenever the model returns nothing.
e: If a field is required but the data often doesn't exist, the schema pushes the model to fabricate. Allowing null removes that pressure. Instructions alone don't fix the conflicting schema, and defaults create wrong data.

q: Your `payment_method` enum is ["card", "bank_transfer"]. Some invoices are paid by check, and they're being labeled "card". What's the best schema change?
o: Add "other" to the enum, with a separate text field to describe it.
Remove the enum and let the model write any value it wants to.
Add a note asking the model to choose the closest available option.
Delete invoices paid by check before they reach the extraction step.
e: An "other" value plus a detail field gives the model an honest option when nothing fits, while keeping the main values structured. Free text loses consistency, and choosing the closest option is what causes mislabeling.

q: With `tool_choice` set to "auto", some extraction responses contain text instead of a tool call. What should you change?
o: Set `tool_choice` to "any" or force the extraction tool, so a tool call is required.
Keep "auto" and write code that parses whatever JSON appears in the text responses.
Raise `max_tokens`, so the model has enough room to produce the tool call.
Lower the temperature, so the model chooses the tool call more consistently.
e: "auto" allows the model to answer in text. Requiring a tool call ("any" or a forced tool) guarantees structured output. Parsing JSON out of text is fragile, and token limits or temperature don't change the choice.

q: Where do you read the extracted data after Claude calls your `extract_contract` tool?
o: In the `input` field of the tool_use block in Claude's response.
In a text block that follows the tool_use block in the response.
In a file that the tool writes to disk automatically after each call.
In the `stop_reason` field, which carries the extracted JSON object.
e: When Claude calls a tool, the arguments it produced are in the tool_use block's `input`. For extraction, that object is your structured data. Nothing is written to disk automatically, and `stop_reason` is just a status value.

q: Your extraction schema has a `notes` field described only as "Notes." The field ends up with random text. What helps most?
o: Describe exactly what belongs in the field and give a short example.
Mark the field as required so the model always fills it in.
Rename it to `NOTES` in capitals so the model treats it as important.
Move it to the top of the schema so it's processed first.
e: Field descriptions guide the model's output. A clear explanation and example make the expected content obvious. Requiring the field or changing capitalization or order doesn't clarify what it should contain.

q: An extracted invoice fails your check because its line items don't add up to the total. What's the best retry?
o: Send back the document, the failed output and the specific error, and ask for a corrected extraction.
Send the same request again unchanged, since the model will probably get it right the second time.
Accept the output as is, because tool use already guarantees the values are correct and consistent.
Change the total in code to match the line items, and skip any retry with the model altogether.
e: A retry with the specific error gives the model what it needs to correct itself. Identical retries repeat the same mistake, tool use doesn't guarantee consistency, and silently changing totals can hide real document issues.

q: Retries for a missing `tax_id` keep failing, and you find the tax ID isn't in the document at all. What should you do?
o: Stop retrying and record the field as missing, since no retry can find absent data.
Retry more times with stronger wording, because the value must be hidden somewhere.
Ask the model to produce a plausible tax ID, so the record passes validation.
Delete the document from the dataset so the failure no longer shows up in reports.
e: Retries help when the model made a fixable mistake, not when the information doesn't exist. Record it as missing (or route it for human follow-up). Pushing harder or inventing a value leads to fabricated data.

q: Which job fits the Message Batches API best?
o: Extracting data from 5,000 archived contracts by the end of the week.
Answering a customer's live chat message within a few seconds.
Running a review that blocks a developer's merge until it finishes.
A workflow that needs several rounds of tool calls in each request.
e: Batches are cheaper but can take up to 24 hours and don't support multi-turn tool use within a request. Large, non-urgent jobs fit well. Live chat and blocking checks need fast responses.

q: What's the main trade-off of the Message Batches API?
o: Lower cost, in exchange for results that may take up to 24 hours.
Faster results, in exchange for paying a higher price per token.
Bigger context windows, in exchange for losing access to tool use.
Better accuracy, in exchange for processing fewer documents.
e: Batch processing costs about half as much, but results can take up to 24 hours. It doesn't make responses faster, increase the context window, or change accuracy.

q: In a batch of 2,000 requests, 40 failed. What's the best way to handle them?
o: Use each failure's `custom_id` to resubmit just those 40, with fixes where needed.
Resubmit all 2,000 requests, so that the results all come from the same run.
Ignore the 40 failures, since 98 percent success is good enough for any job.
Process the 40 by hand, since failed batch requests can never be resubmitted.
e: `custom_id` lets you find exactly which requests failed and resubmit only those, adjusted if the failure had a fixable cause. Rerunning everything wastes money, and ignoring failures leaves gaps.

q: Your team wants to move the pre-merge code review to the Batches API to save money. What's the main problem?
o: Developers would wait up to 24 hours for a review that blocks their merge.
The Batches API can't read code, so it can only review plain English text.
Batches are more expensive than live requests when they process code.
Batch requests can't use a system prompt, so no review criteria can be given.
e: Pre-merge review is a blocking workflow where developers are waiting, so up to 24 hours of latency is unacceptable. Batches fit non-blocking jobs like overnight audits. Batches can process code, cost less, and support system prompts.

q: What's the main benefit of a second, independent Claude instance reviewing generated code?
o: It doesn't share the generator's assumptions, so it catches errors the generator would miss.
It always uses a newer model than the generator, which gives it better knowledge of the code.
It can merge the pull request automatically, so developers don't have to wait for anyone.
It doubles the context window, because both instances share their remaining token space.
e: An independent reviewer approaches the code without the generator's reasoning and is less likely to repeat its blind spots. It's not automatically a newer model, doesn't merge on its own, and contexts aren't pooled.

q: Your large pull request touches the API layer, database, and front end. How can a multi-pass review be organized?
o: Review each area in its own pass, then add a pass that checks how they work together.
Review everything in one pass three times, and keep only the findings that repeat.
Review only the API layer, since bugs in other areas are always caught by tests.
Skip review and rely on developers to report any problems after the code ships.
e: Focused passes on each area give depth, and an integration pass catches issues that span them. Repeating a single unfocused pass doesn't improve depth, and skipping areas or review entirely misses bugs.

q: Your extraction pipeline adds a second pass where a separate instance checks the first pass's output against the source document. What's this good for?
o: Catching extraction errors that the first pass couldn't see in its own work.
Doubling the speed of extraction, since two instances work at the same time.
Guaranteeing zero errors, so that human review can be removed entirely.
Replacing schema validation, since a second instance checks structure too.
e: An independent verification pass catches mistakes the first pass made, improving accuracy. It adds work rather than speed, doesn't guarantee perfection, and complements (not replaces) schema validation.

q: You run two independent review passes. Pass A reports an issue that pass B doesn't. How can you use this?
o: Treat agreement as higher confidence and route disagreements to a human for a closer look.
Always discard any finding that only one pass reported, since it must be a false positive.
Always keep the finding from pass A, because whichever pass finished first is more accurate.
Run passes until they agree, no matter how many runs it takes, before reporting anything.
e: Agreement between independent passes suggests higher confidence, while disagreements are good candidates for human review. Throwing out single-pass findings can drop real bugs, and running until agreement wastes cost.

q: After summarizing a long chat, the agent forgets that the customer's replacement must arrive by May 12. How can you keep facts like this?
o: Keep a structured "case facts" block (dates, amounts, IDs) that is carried forward unchanged.
Summarize more often, so each summary is shorter and easier for the model to remember.
Ask the customer to repeat important details every few messages, just in case.
Raise the temperature so the model recalls more varied details from earlier turns.
e: Progressive summaries tend to blur precise details. A separate structured block of key facts that's preserved verbatim keeps them available. More frequent summaries make the loss worse, and asking customers to repeat themselves is poor service.

q: Your synthesis agent receives 15 findings in one long block, and findings in the middle are often missed. What helps?
o: Put a summary of key findings at the start and organize the rest under clear headings.
Add more findings so the important ones in the middle are less likely to be crowded.
Remove every finding except the first and last, since those are the ones that get used.
Repeat the entire input twice, so that the model gets a second chance to read it all.
e: Long inputs suffer from the "lost in the middle" effect. Leading with a summary and adding clear structure makes the key points easier to use. Adding more content or repeating it wastes context, and dropping findings loses information.

q: Your `get_account` tool returns 60 fields, but the agent only needs 6. Context fills up quickly in long chats. What's the best fix?
o: Trim the tool result to the fields the agent needs before adding it to the conversation.
Increase the model's context window, so the full 60 fields can always fit comfortably.
Call the tool less often, even when the agent needs updated account information.
Ask the model to ignore the fields it doesn't need when it reads each tool result.
e: Trimming verbose tool results to the relevant fields keeps context focused and leaves room for the conversation. Asking the model to ignore fields still spends the tokens, and skipping necessary calls risks stale data.

q: Your chat app resends only the last three turns with each request to save tokens. Customers have to repeat themselves. What's the underlying problem?
o: The API is stateless, so anything left out of the request is unknown to the model.
The model's memory resets every three turns, so this is how all chat apps behave.
Customers write too much, and the model can only follow short conversations.
The system prompt is too short, which makes the model forget earlier turns.
e: The Messages API doesn't remember previous requests. The model only knows what's in the current request. Dropping earlier turns (without a summary or key facts) removes that information.

q: A customer asks for a refund, and the policy has no rule covering their unusual situation. What should the agent do?
o: Escalate to a human, because the policy doesn't cover the case.
Approve the refund, because customers should always be satisfied.
Deny the refund, because anything not covered is not allowed.
Invent a reasonable rule and apply it, to keep the chat moving.
e: Policy gaps are a clear escalation trigger. The agent shouldn't make up policy in either direction. A human can make the judgment call and possibly update the policy.

q: A customer is polite and calm but explicitly asks to speak with a person. What should the agent do?
o: Honor the request and escalate, with a summary of the issue.
Keep trying to solve it first, since the customer is calm.
Ask them to explain why they don't want to use the agent.
Ignore the request unless they ask a second or third time.
e: An explicit request for a human is a direct escalation trigger, regardless of tone. Delaying or questioning it frustrates the customer. Include a summary so the human can pick up smoothly.

q: `lookup_order` finds two orders matching the customer's description, both from the same day. What should the agent do?
o: Ask a short question to identify which order the customer means.
Pick the more expensive order, since it's more likely to matter.
Process both orders, so the customer's issue is definitely covered.
Escalate to a human, since multiple matches always need a person.
e: When there's ambiguity, a targeted clarifying question is the right move. Guessing or acting on both orders risks wrong changes, and escalation isn't needed for something the customer can easily clarify.

q: Why is "escalate when the customer seems angry" a weak rule on its own?
o: Anger doesn't reliably show whether the agent can solve the issue or a human is needed.
The model can't detect emotion in text at all, so the rule would never be triggered.
Angry customers should never be escalated, since humans don't enjoy those calls.
Escalation is expensive, so it should only happen when a customer threatens to leave.
e: Sentiment is a poor proxy for complexity: some angry customers have simple fixes, and some calm ones need a human. Better triggers are explicit requests, policy gaps, and the agent's inability to make progress.

q: One of five search subagents failed, but the final report reads as if the research were complete. What should change?
o: Pass the failure up and have the report note which area has limited coverage and why.
Hide failures from the final report so that readers trust the research findings more.
Abort the whole research task whenever any one subagent fails, to avoid weak reports.
Have the synthesis agent fill in the missing area based on its general knowledge.
e: Failures should propagate with context so the final output can be honest about gaps. Hiding them misleads readers, aborting wastes the good work, and filling gaps with general knowledge mixes unsourced content into a cited report.

q: After hours of exploring a big codebase, Claude starts giving vague answers that don't match the code. What's a likely cause and fix?
o: Context is overloaded; save key findings to a notes file and continue in a fresh context.
The code has changed; re-clone the repository and start the exploration again from zero.
The model is tired; take a break and try again later in the same exact session.
The questions are too hard; ask simpler questions until the answers improve again.
e: Long sessions accumulate noise, and quality drops as context fills. Writing key findings to a file (a scratchpad) and starting fresh with that summary keeps the knowledge while restoring focus.

q: Why have a subagent explore part of a large codebase and return a summary?
o: The verbose exploration stays in the subagent's context, so the main context only gets the summary.
Subagents can read files that the main agent is never allowed to open, for security and sandboxing reasons.
Subagents run on faster hardware, so exploration finishes sooner than in the main agent.
Summaries are always more accurate than the original code, so nothing important is lost.
e: Delegating exploration isolates the noisy discovery work. The main agent keeps a clean context with just what it needs. Subagents don't get special file permissions or hardware, and summaries can lose detail, so they should be focused.
