q: Your session is getting full, and you're not done exploring. Which Claude Code command can condense the conversation while keeping key information?
o: `/compact`
`/clear`
`/init`
`/memory`
e: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to free up space while keeping the important points. `/clear` throws away the history, `/init` sets up a CLAUDE.md file, and `/memory` edits memory files.

q: A multi-hour codebase analysis job sometimes crashes and has to start over. What design helps it recover?
o: Save progress (findings so far, files done) to a file regularly, and resume from it.
Run the whole job in a single request, so it either fully succeeds or fully fails.
Run the job twice in parallel and hope that one of the two copies doesn't crash.
Reduce the job to analyzing only a handful of files, so it always finishes quickly.
e: Checkpointing progress to durable storage lets the job resume where it left off. A single giant request is fragile, parallel duplicates waste cost, and shrinking the scope defeats the purpose.

q: Before splitting a large refactor across subagents, what should the main agent do with its discovery findings?
o: Summarize the relevant findings into each subagent's task so they don't redo discovery.
Send each subagent the entire discovery transcript, so nothing could possibly be missed.
Keep the findings private and let each subagent rediscover what it needs on its own.
Delete the findings, since subagents work better without any prior assumptions.
e: Passing focused, relevant findings saves each subagent from repeating discovery and keeps its context lean. Full transcripts bloat context, and making each subagent rediscover wastes time.

q: While exploring a monorepo, Claude needs to know which packages depend on `shared-utils`. What's an efficient approach?
o: Grep the package manifests for `shared-utils` instead of reading every package.
Read every file in every package to look for any mention of `shared-utils`.
Ask Claude to guess from the package names which ones most likely depend on it.
Delete `shared-utils` and see which packages fail to build afterwards.
e: A targeted search of dependency manifests answers the question quickly without flooding context. Reading everything is wasteful, guessing is unreliable, and deleting code to find dependents is destructive.

q: Your extraction accuracy is 96% overall. Before cutting human review, what should you check?
o: Accuracy broken down by document type and field, since some may be much worse.
Whether 96 is higher than last month's number, since any increase is good enough.
Nothing more, since 96% overall means every document type is at least 96%.
Whether the model says it's confident, since self-reports are well calibrated.
e: An overall number can hide weak segments: one document type or field may be far below average. Check performance by segment before reducing oversight. Model self-reported confidence isn't reliably calibrated.

q: After automating high-confidence extractions, how do you keep track of errors in them?
o: Have humans review a random sample of the automated results on an ongoing basis.
Stop checking them, since high confidence means they're always correct now.
Review only the ones customers complain about, since those are the real errors.
Re-run each one through the model a second time and compare both outputs.
e: Ongoing random sampling measures the real error rate and catches new failure patterns. Complaints are a biased, delayed signal, and re-running the same model shares its blind spots.

q: How should you set the confidence threshold for sending extractions to human review?
o: Calibrate it against a labeled set, so you know the error rate at each threshold.
Pick 90 percent, because it's the standard threshold used across the industry.
Let the model choose its own threshold for each document as it processes it.
Use the same threshold for every field, since all fields have equal risk.
e: Thresholds should be based on measured accuracy at each confidence level, using labeled data. There's no universal correct number, and fields with different risk may need different thresholds.

q: Reviewers can only check 200 extractions a day. Which should they see first?
o: Low-confidence results and high-impact fields, where errors are likeliest and costliest.
The 200 most recent results, since newer documents are more important to the business.
A random 200, so that every result has exactly the same chance of being reviewed.
The 200 longest documents, since longer documents always contain more errors.
e: With limited capacity, review where errors are most likely and most costly. Random sampling has a role in measuring accuracy, but for catching errors, prioritizing by risk is more effective.

q: Your agent asks reviewers to approve refunds with only "Approve? yes/no." They rubber-stamp almost everything. What improves review quality?
o: Show the key facts, the policy that applies, and why the case was flagged.
Make reviewers wait 30 seconds before the approve button becomes active.
Ask reviewers to approve fewer refunds each day, regardless of their merits.
Remove human review, since reviewers just approve everything anyway.
e: Reviewers can only judge well if they see the relevant evidence and the reason for review. Delays and quotas don't add information, and removing review loses the safeguard.

q: Your model's field-level confidence for `due_date` is high, but sampled reviews show it's often wrong for one supplier's invoices. What does this suggest?
o: Confidence isn't well calibrated for that segment, so route it to review until it's fixed.
The human reviewers must be the ones making mistakes, since the model's confidence is so high.
That supplier's invoices are fake, so they should be rejected without any review.
Confidence scores are useless everywhere, so the whole system should be shut down.
e: High confidence with poor real accuracy shows a calibration problem in that segment. Route it to human review while you improve it (for example with examples of that supplier's format). It doesn't mean the reviewers are wrong or the whole system is useless.

q: Two reputable sources give different market sizes: $4.2B and $5.1B. How should the report handle it?
o: Report both, cite each, and note possible reasons for the difference.
Average them to $4.65B and cite both sources for that figure.
Pick the larger number, since bigger numbers are usually more recent.
Leave the figure out, since conflicting data can't be reported.
e: Presenting both with attribution, and noting why they may differ (different years, definitions, methods), gives readers an honest picture. Averaging creates a number nobody reported, and picking one arbitrarily hides the conflict.

q: Your summarization step drops source links, so the report can't cite anything. What's the fix?
o: Keep each claim paired with its source through every step, using structured output.
Add sources back at the end by searching the web for each claim in the report.
Cite "various sources" at the bottom of the report as a general reference.
Remove the summarization step, since summaries can never include sources.
e: Provenance must be carried through the pipeline, so each step keeps claim-source pairs. Re-searching after the fact can attach the wrong source, and vague citations don't let readers verify claims.

q: Two sources disagree on a statistic, but one is from 2018 and the other from 2025. What should the report do?
o: Note the dates and treat the difference as possible change over time, not just a contradiction.
Always report the older figure, since older sources have had more time to be checked by others.
Report them as a direct contradiction, without mentioning when each was published.
Ignore both figures, since sources from different years can't be compared at all.
e: Including publication dates lets the report distinguish real conflicts from change over time. Labeling it a contradiction without dates misleads readers.

q: Some findings in your report are well established and others are contested. How should the report present them?
o: Separate them clearly and state the level of support or dispute for each.
Present everything with the same confidence so the report reads smoothly.
Leave out every contested finding so the report only has certain claims.
Put contested findings first, since they're more interesting to readers.
e: Readers need to know which claims are solid and which are debated. Uniform confidence misleads, dropping contested findings loses useful information, and ordering by interest doesn't communicate certainty.

q: One source's key evidence is a table of figures; another is a direct quote from a regulator. How should synthesis handle them?
o: Keep each in a fitting form: the figures as a table and the quote word for word, with citations.
Paraphrase both into short bullet points, so the whole report has one consistent and readable writing style.
Drop the table and keep only the quote, since quotes are always more reliable than data.
Convert the quote into a number, so it can be compared directly with the table figures.
e: Some content loses meaning when paraphrased. Tables keep figures precise, and exact quotes matter for regulatory statements. Flattening everything into bullets risks distortion.

q: Your extraction combines data from an invoice and a matching purchase order, and their amounts differ. What should the output do?
o: Record both values with their source document, and flag the mismatch for review.
Use the invoice amount, since invoices are always correct and POs are drafts.
Average the two amounts, so the output reflects both of the documents fairly.
Drop the amount field entirely, so the record doesn't contain conflicting data.
e: Keeping both values with their source and flagging the conflict preserves the facts and sends the issue to someone who can resolve it. Picking one by rule, averaging, or dropping the field hides a real discrepancy.
